answer_text:
Let

\[
M=\max_{x\in[0,1]} |f'(x)|.
\]

If \(f\equiv 0\), the inequality is trivial, so assume \(f\not\equiv 0\). Since \(f(0)=0\),

\[
|f(x)|=\left|\int_0^x f'(t)\,dt\right|\le Mx.
\]

Also, since \(f(1)=0\),

\[
|f(x)|=\left|-\int_x^1 f'(t)\,dt\right|\le M(1-x).
\]

Therefore, for every \(x\in[0,1]\),

\[
|f(x)|\le M\min(x,1-x).
\]

Integrating gives

\[
\int_0^1 |f(x)|\,dx
\le M\int_0^1 \min(x,1-x)\,dx.
\]

Now

\[
\int_0^1 \min(x,1-x)\,dx
=
\int_0^{1/2}x\,dx+\int_{1/2}^1(1-x)\,dx
=
\frac18+\frac18
=
\frac14.
\]

Hence

\[
\int_0^1 |f(x)|\,dx\le \frac{M}{4},
\]

so

\[
M\ge 4\int_0^1 |f(x)|\,dx.
\]

Thus \(C=4\) works.

To show that no larger constant can work, consider the \(C^1\) family

\[
f_\varepsilon(x)=
\begin{cases}
x, & 0\le x\le \frac12-\varepsilon,\\[4pt]
\frac12-\varepsilon+\frac{2\varepsilon}{\pi}
\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2\varepsilon}\left(x-\frac12+\varepsilon\right)\right),
& \frac12-\varepsilon\le x\le \frac12+\varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1-x, & \frac12+\varepsilon\le x\le 1,
\end{cases}
\]

for \(0<\varepsilon<\frac14\). This function satisfies \(f_\varepsilon(0)=f_\varepsilon(1)=0\), is continuously differentiable, and

\[
\max_{x\in[0,1]} |f_\varepsilon'(x)|=1.
\]

As \(\varepsilon\to 0^+\), \(f_\varepsilon\) converges uniformly to the triangular function

\[
f_0(x)=
\begin{cases}
x, & 0\le x\le \frac12,\\
1-x, & \frac12\le x\le 1,
\end{cases}
\]

so

\[
\int_0^1 |f_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx\to \int_0^1 |f_0(x)|\,dx=\frac14.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{\max |f_\varepsilon'|}{\int_0^1 |f_\varepsilon|}
=
\frac{1}{\int_0^1 |f_\varepsilon|}
\to 4.
\]

Thus any \(C>4\) fails for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). Hence the largest possible constant is

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
